newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria gives guidelines for March council poll.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria gives guidelines for March council poll.

text.p: Nigeria's electoral commission NECON on Friday released guidelines for aspirants and voters for local council polls fixed for March 15 -- next step in a phased return to full democracy from military rule.
NECON chairman Sumner Dagogo-Jack told a news conference in the capital Abuja that there would be two different elections simultaneously on the same day nationwide.

"These are the election of one councilor for each of the 8,184 wards in the various local government areas and areas councils and the election of chairman for each of the 774 local government area councils in the country," Dagogo-Jack said.
The poll should have been held in December but were shifted by NECON who blame the delay on the creation of six new states and 183 new council areas in October.
NECON maintains the rescheduled poll, the first to test the strength of the five registered political parties, would not affect the rest of the programme to install democracy.
Nigeria is shunned worldwide for lack of democracy and alleged human rights violations.
It was suspended from the Commonwealth, which groups Britain and its former colonies following the hanging of nine minority rights activists in 1995 including author Ken Saro-Wiwa.
The Commonwealth gave Nigeria up to this year to restore democracy, a directive military ruler General Sani Abacha has ignored and is instead following his own democratisation plan.
Dagogo-Jack said aspirants for chairmen and councillors in the poll must, in addition to attaining secondary school education, be not less than 35 and 25 years old, respectively.
He said voting, to be held between a period of 8.00 am (0700 gmt) and 4.00 pm (1500 gmt), would be by secret ballot at the country's 101,151 polling centres.
Voters must be Nigerian citizens, 18 years and above, resident in the ward where they intend to vote and carry a valid registration card of that ward, he said.
A 10-day registration of voters for the poll ended on Wednesday dogged by complaints of fraud and inadequate materials.
Nigeria's last attempt at democracy ended in chaos when the previous military ruler annulled a presidential vote in 1993.
Moshood Abiola, the presumed winner of the annulled poll is in detention and so are many other opposition figures.
